title_options: This Bird Flew 11 Days Without Landing. Then It Turned the Wrong Way
A 4-Month-Old Bird Flew 13,560 km Nonstop. Nobody Showed It the Way
We Checked the Wind Behind the Longest Bird Flight Ever Recorded

lines.text: In October 2022, a bird that was about four months old took off from Alaska.
For the next eleven days, it did not land. Not once.
It crossed at least 13,560 kilometers of open Pacific.
This story is usually told as a miracle of the body. The satellite tag on its back recorded something stranger.
Near the end, the bird turned toward a place it was never supposed to go.
Summer 2022. The tundra of the Seward Peninsula, near Nome, Alaska.
Biologists from the U.S. Geological Survey were searching the grass for bar-tailed godwit chicks.
The chicks are small, scattered and hard to see against the tundra.
A few of them got a satellite tag that weighs about five grams, powered by a tiny solar panel.
One young bird carried a leg flag with a short code: B6.
On two of the other chicks, the tags slipped off. They kept transmitting from the grass, going nowhere.
Then the adults left.
Adult godwits leave Alaska weeks before their young. The juveniles make their first migration on their own.
No leader. No map. No practice flight over the ocean.
B6 moved south to the coastal mudflats of western Alaska and fed for weeks.
Godwits on these flats eat clams, worms and berries, and they put on fat fast.
Studies of adults show what happens next. Before departure, more than half of the body weight can be fat.
The gut and liver shrink, and the heart and flight muscles grow.
In 2007, a tagged adult female, known as E7, flew about 11,700 kilometers from Alaska to New Zealand in roughly eight days. It was the first nonstop crossing ever tracked.
That part is famous. The part that matters more is simpler.
A godwit cannot rest on the sea. It has no webbed feet, and it is not built to take off from water.
So once it leaves the coast, it flaps, day and night, until it reaches land on the other side.
Which raises a practical question. When do you leave?
Tracking of adult godwits suggests they do not just wait for a calm day.
They tend to leave on winds that help them across the whole ocean, not only at takeoff.
How a bird reads weather thousands of kilometers away is still not known.
On October 13th, B6 left Alaska.
It flew south, out over the Aleutian Islands, and into open water.
It passed west of Hawaii without stopping.
Around October 19th, it crossed Kiribati, near the equator.
A couple of days later it was over Vanuatu, then New Caledonia.
Islands. Beaches. Food. It flew past all of them.
Here is one number we worked out ourselves. 13,560 kilometers in 11 days and 1 hour is about 51 kilometers per hour, on average, around the clock.
How much of that speed was the bird, and how much was the sky?
B6's raw track is not public, so we rebuilt an approximate route from the published waypoints and checked it against a global weather model.
At about 1,500 meters, the wind along that route blew the bird's way about nine hours out of ten.
On average, that is roughly 20 kilometers per hour of free push, strongest in the north and weakest near the equator.
That is not luck. The route follows the big wind belts of the Pacific.
Then, near the end, the wind stopped explaining things.
Alaskan godwits usually fly to New Zealand or eastern Australia.
B6 went past them. It passed about 600 kilometers off Sydney, still heading south.
It reached the latitude of New Zealand, far to the west of it.
On October 23rd, it turned sharply west, toward Tasmania.
So which was it? A youngster blown off course, or a bird that knew where it was going?
One researcher suggested strong easterly winds pushed it west.
We looked at the weather model at the turn. On the morning of the 23rd, the wind there came mostly from the north.
It pushed south, not west. Winds from the northeast arrived later that day and helped it the rest of the way.
So the wind can explain why it overshot. It does not clearly explain the turn.
Our route is approximate, so treat that as a clue, not a verdict.
The honest answer is that nobody knows yet.
Researchers do not know how often young godwits take this route. It could be common. It could be rare.
Here is what is certain. 13,560 kilometers. Eleven days and one hour. No food, no water, no rest on the sea.
The previous record belonged to an adult male, at about 12,200 kilometers.
B6 beat it on its very first migration.
It came down at Ansons Bay, in northeast Tasmania, having likely lost about half of its body weight.
How it slept up there, nobody has measured.
A bird that was never shown the way changed what scientists thought a young godwit could do.
